title: Jonah and Nineveh
lead: God gives a second chance both to a disobedient prophet and to a city that did not deserve one.
questions: Who is your Nineveh, and what does your first reaction to the thought that God wants to save it say about you?
Do you bargain with God like Abraham, to save people, or like Jonah, to make sure the sentence falls after all?
When did someone’s conversion or success last sting you instead of making you glad, and what did you do with that?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: In the book of Jonah, everyone comes off well except the prophet: the sailors pray, the king repents, the city turns around, and the fish, the worm, and the wind obey God at once. The only character who resists is the prophet. Sent to Nineveh, a great city of Assyria, he “got up to flee to Tarshish, away from the presence of the LORD.” During the storm he sleeps below deck, until a pagan captain wakes him with the very words the Creator used to call him: “Get up and call upon your God.” The prophet ran from the word of the LORD, but the word of the LORD caught up with him: he heard it from the mouth of a pagan. Jonah recites a flawless confession about the Maker of sea and land while fleeing from Him across the sea. You can have perfect doctrine and be sailing in the opposite direction.

The great fish is not a punishment: the prayer from its belly is a psalm of thanksgiving from a man who has been rescued, not the lament of a prisoner. God slipped a drowning deserter his last lifeline, and then “the word of the LORD came to Jonah a second time.” The same command, the same messenger: a second chance for the prophet before he carries a second chance to the city. The shortest sermon in the Bible, “Forty more days and Nineveh will be overturned!”, contains a verb with two meanings: to overthrow, or to turn around. The second came true: the city turned around. The king got up from his throne, just as Jonah had gotten up to run, and sat in ashes with a hope as small as a seed: “Who knows? God may turn and relent.” It was enough. God withdrew the sentence in words almost identical to those with which He once spared Israel after the golden calf. He treated the enemies exactly as He had treated His own.

That is what the prophet could not bear. He revealed why he had run: “I knew that You are a gracious and compassionate God.” Jonah is the only person in the Bible who quotes the Sinai revelation of grace as an accusation. He rejoiced in his own rescue and in the shade of a plant; he was angered by someone else’s deliverance and by the loss of his comfort. The book ends with God’s question: should He not care about a city of more than a hundred and twenty thousand people? There is no answer, because the reader is meant to write it. Of all possible signs, Jesus promised only one: the sign of Jonah. The second chance in this story really is for everyone.

The book of Jonah is short, funny, and merciless, just not toward those we think deserve it. All the pagans in it come off well: the sailors pray, the captain reminds Jonah of God, the king repents, the city turns around, and even the fish, the worm, and the wind follow orders without grumbling. The only character who resists the Creator for four chapters is the prophet. This is not a book about a wicked city. It is a mirror handed to God’s people. It takes courage to look into it.

sections.heading: The Good-News Prophet
paragraphs: Jonah was not just anybody. He was the one who announced to Jeroboam II that Israel’s borders would be restored. His words came true: the country expanded and prospered. Jonah had preached nothing but good news to his people, until God said to him: “Get up! Go to the great city of Nineveh and preach against it.” Nineveh was one of the most important cities of Assyria, though it became the empire’s capital only later. Israel had every reason to fear the Assyrian war machine. So Jonah got up (the text uses the same verb, only in the opposite direction) “to flee to Tarshish, away from the presence of the LORD.” To the far end of the known world. The narrator chose his words carefully: Jonah flees “away from the presence of the LORD.” In the Old Testament only one other man did the same: Cain. To place a prophet in the same line as the first murderer is a strong hint of how serious this disobedience was. And we will learn the reason for his flight only at the end. It will turn out to be the strangest reason in the history of desertion.

sections.heading: The Captain’s Sermon
paragraphs: A storm broke out at sea. The sailors cried out to their gods and threw the cargo overboard, while the only worshiper of the true God on board lay fast asleep below deck. It happens: a person in open disobedience can sleep soundly, so peace in itself is not yet proof that we are on the right road. A pagan captain woke him with words that should have chilled him to the bone: “Get up and call upon your God.” In Hebrew these are exactly the two verbs with which God had called him: get up, call out. The prophet ran from the word of the LORD, but the word of the LORD caught up with him: he heard it from the mouth of a pagan. God can speak through people outside the circle of the initiated, and He does so especially readily when the initiated are asleep. Then the sailors cast lots, asked a few questions, and Jonah introduced himself without a stammer: “I am a Hebrew… I worship the LORD, the God of the heavens, who made the sea and the dry land.” Theologically impeccable. Except that he made this confession on a ship on which he was fleeing from the Maker of the sea, across the sea. You can have flawless doctrine and be sailing in exactly the opposite direction. And when the sailors heard the sentence Jonah had passed on himself, they did something that put the prophet to shame: they did not want to throw him overboard. They “rowed hard to get back to dry land,” risking their lives for a stranger who had brought disaster on them. Pagans fought harder for the life of a stranger than God’s prophet did.

sections.heading: The Fish Is Not a Punishment
paragraphs: When Jonah was finally thrown into the sea and began to drown, “the LORD had appointed a great fish.” We are used to reading the fish as a punishment, a grim prison with a moral. The text says something else, and it says it through its literary form: the prayer from inside the fish is a psalm of thanksgiving, not a lament. “In my distress I called to the LORD, and He answered me… But You raised my life from the pit, O LORD my God!” That is not how a prisoner prays. That is how a rescued man prays. The fish is not a cell; it is the last lifeline God slipped to a drowning deserter. One more thing is worth stressing: Jonah prays in phrases from the book of Psalms, fluently, from memory. He knew how to pray properly, and he knew his theology very well. Knowledge was not his problem. Right after the prophet’s prayer comes the sentence on which this whole book rests: “the word of the LORD came to Jonah a second time.” A second time. The same command, the same city, the same messenger. God did not swap the prophet for a more capable one. He gave a second chance to the one who had failed, before sending him with a second chance for others. Whoever carries to someone the news of God’s patience has probably just experienced it themselves.

sections.heading: The City That Got Up
paragraphs: So Jonah goes to Nineveh and preaches the shortest sermon in the Bible: “Forty more days and Nineveh will be overturned!” The Hebrew verb in this sentence has two meanings: to overthrow, to turn upside down, as with Sodom, but also to turn around, to change into something else. Jonah meant the first. The second came true: in forty days Nineveh was transformed. “And the Ninevites believed God. They proclaimed a fast and dressed in sackcloth, from the greatest of them to the least.” The news reaches the king, and the text plays with a verb again: when the word of the LORD reached Jonah, he got up to run away; when it reached the pagan king, “he got up from his throne, took off his royal robe, covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in ashes.” The same verb, two directions of the heart. The royal decree then goes so far that we smile despite the seriousness of the scene: “Let no man or beast, herd or flock, taste anything at all,” and “let both man and beast be covered with sackcloth.” The pagan ruler knows no theology of repentance, so he does everything he can to show it. And his hope is astonishingly modest: “Who knows? God may turn and relent.” No certainty, no promise in hand. “Who knows?” was enough. Sometimes all the faith a person can manage fits into those two words, and God accepts it. And when the Lord sees their repentance, the narrator describes His response in words almost identical to those from the day of the golden calf, when the Almighty relented from destroying His own people. The grace Israel had received now became Nineveh’s. God did not deal more gently with His own than with His enemies. He treated them exactly the same. And that is precisely what Jonah could not bear.

sections.heading: The Evil That Remained
paragraphs: In Hebrew, the last chapters of this book are held together by one word: evil. The king orders the people to turn from their evil ways. His subjects do it. God relents from the evil He had announced (our translation says “disaster”). But Jonah “was greatly displeased”; literally, it was evil to him, a great evil. The only evil left in this story after Nineveh’s conversion lives in the prophet’s heart. And at last Jonah reveals why he ran: “I knew that You are a gracious and compassionate God, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion.” This is a literal quotation from Sinai, from the moment when God revealed His name to Moses. Israel repeated this formula for centuries in psalms and prayers, always to praise the Creator. Jonah is the only person in the Bible who quotes it as an accusation. He did not run because he did not know God. He ran because he knew Him too well: he knew that if the Almighty sent him with a sentence and Nineveh repented, He would forgive. He wanted justice for his enemies, and grace for himself and his own. The prophet asks to die. In the fish he prayed for life; now he prays for death, not because he has lost something, but because others have been saved. In the story from two days ago, Elijah sat under a similar desert bush with the same request on his lips, but with an entirely different heart: Elijah wanted to die because people had rejected his message. Jonah wants to die because they accepted it.

sections.heading: Two Men Sitting and One Plant
paragraphs: At the end the narrator leaves us a picture built out of two mirrors. In the middle of the city sits the king: in dust and ashes, hoping for deliverance. Outside the walls sits the prophet: in a shelter, hoping for destruction, because he “sat in its shade to see what would happen to the city.” The same posture, opposite prayers. Then God begins His last lesson, taught entirely with props: a plant springs up and gives shade, “and Jonah was greatly pleased with the plant.” The next day a worm attacks the plant, the east wind and the sun torment the prophet, and once again he thinks it would be better to die. The arithmetic of this book is brutally simple. Two things make Jonah glad: his own deliverance and his own shade. Two things make him angry: someone else’s deliverance and the loss of his own comfort. Throughout the book, the wind, the fish, the plant, and the worm obey God immediately, unlike the prophet. Creatures that know no theology turn out to be more obedient than a man with a complete theological education.

sections.heading: A Question Without an Answer
paragraphs: In the last chapter God asks three questions. Jonah answers only one, and defiantly: “I am angry enough to die!” The book ends with God’s final question: “You cared about the plant, which you neither tended nor made grow… So should I not care about the great city of Nineveh, which has more than 120,000 people who cannot tell their right hand from their left, and many cattle as well?” And that is the end. There is no answer from Jonah, because this book is not waiting for his. It is waiting for ours. Long ago Abraham bargained with God over pagan Sodom, all the way down to ten righteous people, just to save it. Jonah bargained over Nineveh in the opposite direction. Every believer carries on one of these two bargains in life, and it is worth checking which one. And Jesus, asked for a sign, refused every sign but one: “the sign of the prophet Jonah.” Three days in the heart of the earth, as that prophet was in the fish. God’s greatest sign bears the name of the most stubborn of the prophets. Apparently the second chance in this story really is for everyone.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: If today you are Nineveh, someone who knows they have earned the sentence, this book says that between the announcement and the execution God leaves forty days precisely so that it will not come to that. The Lord would rather see repentance than sentences carried out. For most of us, church people, this book has a harder question: who is my Nineveh? Whom have I quietly crossed off from the reach of grace, because they hurt too much, went too far, are too foreign? Do I rejoice in my own rescue and comfort, while someone else’s deliverance stirs something in me I would rather not admit? The God of this book gives a second chance to the city, to the prophet, and also to the reader who recognizes themselves in Jonah. The book ends with a question, because we are meant to write the answer with our lives.
